title: Oncall Mentor Guides and Public Incident Templates
author: Maya Chen
content:
Summary
This playbook bundles three related areas we frequently ask responders to consult during and after incidents: (1) an on-call mentor program that accelerates new responders to solo readiness, (2) responder orchestration patterns (how to form a bridge, when to escalate, and how to run cross-functional swarms), and (3) ready-to-use public-facing status page and customer notice templates. The goal: reduce decision latency, standardize external comms, and ensure every incident produces a clear post-incident learning path.

Who this is for
- New and shadowing responders (SREs, serving-runtime engineers, platform, and support).
- Incident commanders, bridge operators, and on-call mentors.
- Customer-facing teams drafting status updates (Support, Customer Success, Trust).

Table of Contents
1) On-call mentor program overview
2) Responder orchestration and bridge formation pattern
3) Runbook invocation matrix
4) Severity classification and immediate actions
5) Customer-status templates (status page + email + twitter-ready)
6) Game day syllabus for mentor-led shadow exercises
7) Postmortem handoff checklist and artifact requirements
8) Ownership and maintenance cadence

1) On-call mentor program overview
Purpose
- Speed up new on-callers from shadowing to confident solo operator in ~8 weeks.
- Provide a lightweight, repeatable checklist mentors use during shadow shifts and after-call reviews.

Program structure
- 2-week onboarding block: documentation walkthrough, synthetic smoke tests, runbook reading.
- 6-week shadowing cycle: each new on-caller shadows 12 shifts (~2 weeks night/weekend coverage). Each shift includes a mentor on the bridge for the first 3 incidents and a mentor wrap-up after shift end.
- Graduation gate: run a solo shift with mentor available on pager escalation only. Mentor signs off using the Solo-Ready checklist.

Mentor responsibilities (short):
- Pre-shift: confirm runbooks and responder roster; run the smoke test notebook for local environment.
- During-shift: coach decision-making, validate severity classification, ensure evidence captured, author customer comm drafts if needed.
- Post-shift: complete a 20-minute micro-retro with the mentee and record two learning items.

Solo-Ready checklist (mentor sign-off)
- Can identify the top three telemetry signals for a platform degradation (latency, error-rate, capacity).
- Can open and follow a primary runbook to mitigate a throttling event.
- Can run core diagnostic commands (see appendix) and interpret results.
- Can draft a clear status update and route it to Support & CS for review.

2) Responder orchestration and bridge formation pattern
When to form a bridge
- Any event classified as Sev1 or Sev2 (see severity section).
- When an incident has >30 minutes of customer-visible downtime or an unclear root cause.
- Multi-service impact (API layer + runtime + infra) where cross-team coordination is required.

Bridge roles and quick definitions
- Bridge Lead (usually Incident Commander): owns the timeline, decisions, and exec brief.
- Bridge Operator: manages the call, status page updates, recordkeeping (timeline entries).
- Triage Lead: runs evidence collection and initial containment actions.
- Subject Matter Leads (SMLs): serving runtime, infra, networking, DB, quantization/kernel.
- Customer Liaison: drafts public templates and coordinates with CS/Support.

Bridge formation checklist (first 10 minutes)
1. Confirm severity & customer impact.
2. Assign Bridge Lead and Bridge Operator.
3. Spin the bridge (Zoom link + recording + shared doc).
4. Triage Lead kicks off evidence collection: metrics dashboards, logs, queue/backlog traces.
5. Post initial TTL (10m) note to status page draft channel.

Bridge run cadence (example)
- 0-10m: rapid triage and containment attempts.
- 10-30m: focused mitigation workstreams and early fallback decisions (route to warm-model variant, reduce feature flag rollout).
- 30-60m: evaluate customer impact; prepare customer notice and Exec brief.
- 60m+: run iterative restores, regression tests, and decision gates for rollback or further mitigation.

3) Runbook invocation matrix
We rely on a small set of canonical runbooks. This matrix explains WHEN to invoke which runbook and WHO must be on-call.

Simple ASCII table:
| Symptom | Primary runbook | On-call owner | Escalation chain |
|---|---|---|---|
| API p95 > 500ms for >10m and error-rate increase | api-latency-throttling | serving-runtime | infra -> SRE lead |
| Elevated kv-cache miss rate + tail latency | kv-cache-eviction-playbook | runtime-cache-sme | runtime lead -> performance eng |
| GPU pool saturating, queue length > 2x | gpu-capacity-throttle-runbook | gpu-fleet-oncall | infra -> dedicated ops |

Invocation rules (bullets)
- If multiple runbooks apply, prioritize the one that limits customer impact fastest.
- If mitigation requires cross-team changes (networking, infra flags), form a bridge.
- Always record invocation in the incident timeline with runbook name and steps taken.

4) Severity classification and immediate actions
Severity definitions (engineered for multi-tenant LLM inference workloads):
- Sev1 (Critical): Broad outage or degraded responses preventing critical functionality for >1% of active customers or traffic. Immediate bridge; exec paging.
- Sev2 (High): Major functionality degraded (>5x latency or >2x error-rate for a subset of customers), customer-visible but partial. Bridge recommended.
- Sev3 (Medium): Localized degradation affecting limited customers or single-region noisy neighbor. Runbook and on-call handling.
- Sev4 (Low): Observability anomaly, minor SLO drift, or feature-specific regression; track and schedule remediation.

Immediate action checklist (first 15 minutes)
1. Acknowledge and timestamp the alert.
2. Triage to determine affected customer impact and scope (sample query, sample payload).
3. Decide bridge/no-bridge and assign roles.
4. Kick off mitigation runbook(s).
5. Draft and publish an initial status page stub (template below).

5) Customer-status templates
Status page best practices
- Use plain language, avoid internal jargon.
- State impact, affected services, and an approximate ETA for next update when known.
- Link to a customer contact for elevated support needs (CS ticket link or customer-specific channel).

Template A: Initial public status page (short)
- Title: "Degraded responses from Redwood Inference API"
- Impact: "Customers may experience increased latency and intermittent errors in text generation and chat endpoints in us-west-2."
- Time detected: 2029-01-10 14:12 UTC
- Current status: "Investigating"
- Next update: "We will provide an update within 30 minutes."
- Contact: "Support: https://redwood.ai/support (include customer ticket # if provided)"

Template B: Customer email for partial-impact incidents
Subject: "Redwood Inference — Partial service degradation affecting API responses"
Body:
Hello <CustomerName>,
We’re writing to let you know we are investigating an issue affecting inference latency in <region>. Some requests may take longer than usual or return 503 errors. Our engineering team has identified the likely cause and is working on a mitigation.
What we know:
- Impacted endpoints: text-generation, chat; embeddings unaffected.
- Regions: us-west-2 reported first; other regions under review.
- What we’re doing: routing traffic to warm model variants and increasing GPU pool capacity.
Estimated next update: 30 minutes.
If this incident affects your SLA tolerance or you need immediate assistance, please reply to this message or open a ticket at https://redwood.ai/support.
Thanks for your patience,
Redwood Inference Operations

Template C: Short social (X/Twitter) update
"We're investigating increased latency and intermittent errors for Redwood Inference API in us-west-2. Engineers are working on mitigation. Status: https://status.redwood.ai — next update in 30m."

Customer notice guidance
- Draft notices should be created by Customer Liaison with input from SMLs.
- CS/Support must approve public emails before send for Sev1/Sev2 incidents.
- Include a clear path for priority customer contact (email + shared Zoom).

6) Game day syllabus for mentor-led shadow exercises
Purpose: validate the mentor program and ensure operators can run the full bridge lifecycle.
Duration: 2 hours per session (1.5 hour exercise + 30m retro).
Participants: 1 mentor, 2 shadow responders, 1 SRE lead, 1 CS liaison.

Scenario examples (rotate monthly):
- Scenario A (KV cache eviction + tail latency): simulate sudden kv-cache misses causing p95 spikes; require participants to enable cache priming fallback and rewrite a status update.
- Scenario B (GPU saturation + noisy neighbor): spinning synthetic load on a tenant causing queueing; participants exercise capacity fencing and burst autoscaler policy.
- Scenario C (Silent regression in model output quality): detect via quality monitors; triage to canary model rollback.

Exercise script (succinct)
1. 0-10m: Incident injection and alerting; mentor ensures timeline activated.
2. 10-30m: Shadow responders classify severity and invoke runbooks.
3. 30-60m: Execute mitigation; generate status page and customer email draft.
4. 60-90m: Restore and evidence collection.
5. 90-120m: 30m retro with action items; mentor records outcomes in onboarding tracker.

Scoring rubric (pass/fail minimum)
- Pass if: timeline created, status page published within 20m, mitigation performed that reduces customer impact by >50% within 60m, and micro-retro completed.

7) Postmortem handoff checklist and artifact requirements
All postmortems must include these artifacts before being moved to the learning backlog:
- Incident timeline (timestamps, decisions, runbooks invoked).
- Customer communications (status page snapshots, emails, social posts).
- Evidence: dashboards or raw query outputs showing the key signal changes (CSV or snapshot images).
- Root cause hypothesis and experiments run.
- Action items (owner, due date, verification plan).

Postmortem template (short)
- Title: [SevX] Short description — Date
- Summary: 3-line executive summary
- Impact: customers, regions, duration
- Timeline: ordered events with timestamps
- Root cause and evidence
- Remediation and action items
- Lessons learned and follow-ups

Artifact retention and regulatory evidence
- For enterprise customers with audit requirements, attach the evidence bundle (logs, S3 archive of timeline doc) and notify the Compliance team within 72 hours.

8) Ownership and maintenance cadence
- Owner: Incident Playbooks guild (rotating owners from SRE, serving-runtime, and platform).
- Quarterly review: every runbook and public template reviewed with at least one SML and one CS rep.
- Game day schedule: mentor-led scenarios run monthly; cross-team long exercises quarterly.

Appendix: Diagnostic command snippets and dashboards
- core diagnostic queries (examples):
  - Check model-server stdout errors: curl -s http://{host}:3100/metrics | grep error_count
  - GPU utilization quick: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,temperature.gpu --format=csv -l 1 -f gpu-dump.csv
  - Queue depth across serving pods: kubectl get hpa -n inference --output=jsonpath='{.items[*].status.currentMetrics}'

Dashboards to consult (ordered):
1. Platform-wide latency overview (p50/p95/p99 by endpoint)
2. GPU pool utilization and queue length (by cluster)
3. KV cache hit/miss rates and eviction counters
4. Rate-limiter and quota throttle counters

Contact and maintenance log
- Document owner: Incident Playbooks guild (playbooks@redwood.ai)
- Last major revision: 2029-01-10 (mentor program updated to add gated sign-off)
- Next review due: 2029-04-01

End of document
